ponder.//: Showcase: one animation per method, from a one-liner (isBetween) to recursion (factorial). Canvas is 1000 x 600.

clamp-int.title: How clamp() works
clamp-int.description: Keeps a number inside the range [minimum, maximum].

slides.caption: clamp(value, minimum, maximum) keeps a number inside a range.
Take value = -4. It is below the minimum, so it falls outside the range.
Too small! The result is the minimum: clamp(-4, 0, 10) = 0.
Now value = 14. It is above the maximum.
Too large! The result is the maximum: clamp(14, 0, 10) = 10.
A value already inside the range is returned unchanged: clamp(6, 0, 10) = 6.

is-between.//: The simplest kind: a few slides that play by themselves (autoAdvance).
is-between.title: How isBetween() works
is-between.description: True if minimum <= value <= maximum. Both ends count.

slides.caption: isBetween(value, minimum, maximum) answers one question: is value inside [minimum, maximum]?
value = 1 is below the minimum 3, so the answer is false.
value = 5 lies between 3 and 7: true.
value = 7 is exactly the maximum. The ends are included, so this is true as well.
value = 9 is above the maximum: false.

gcd.//: Euclid's algorithm. Lengths are 10 px per unit, bars start at x = 150.
gcd.title: How gcd() works
gcd.description: Euclid's algorithm: replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.

slides.caption: gcd(a, b) is the largest number that divides both a and b. Euclid's trick: replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
Lay b along a: 18 fits into 48 two times.
12 is left over. So gcd(48, 18) is the same as gcd(18, 12).
Repeat with a = 18 and b = 12.
12 fits into 18 once and 6 is left over: gcd(18, 12) = gcd(12, 6).
Repeat with a = 12 and b = 6.
6 fits into 12 exactly twice. Nothing is left over: the remainder is 0.
The remainder is 0, so the last b is the answer: gcd(48, 18) = 6.

binary-search.//: Cells are 80 px apart: index i is at x = 140 + 80 * i.
binary-search.title: How binarySearch() works
binary-search.description: Finds a key in a sorted array by halving the search range.

actors.//: A pointer is a group (arrow + label), so moving the group's x moves both.

slides.caption: binarySearch looks for a key in a sorted array by cutting the search range in half each step. We look for 23; lo and hi mark the range.
Check the middle: mid = (0 + 9) / 2 = 4, and sorted[4] = 16.
16 < 23, so 23 can only be to the right of mid. Drop the left half: lo = mid + 1 = 5.
New middle: mid = (5 + 9) / 2 = 7, and sorted[7] = 56.
56 > 23, so 23 can only be to the left of mid. Drop the right part: hi = mid - 1 = 6.
mid = (5 + 6) / 2 = 5, and sorted[5] = 23.
Found it: binarySearch returns 5, after only 3 comparisons for 10 elements.

palindrome.//: Letters are 80 px apart: index i is at x = 260 + 80 * i.
palindrome.title: How isPalindrome() works
palindrome.description: Two pointers walk towards each other and compare letters.

slides.caption: isPalindrome(s) checks whether s reads the same forwards and backwards, with two pointers that walk towards each other.
i starts at the first letter, j at the last: 'r' and 'r' are equal.
Move both inwards: 'a' and 'a' are equal.
'c' and 'c' are equal.
The pointers meet in the middle and every pair matched, so the answer is true.
Now try "racecat": only the last letter is different.
'r' and 't' differ, so the method returns false right away. The other letters are never checked.

//: Each bar is a group (rectangle + number) so it moves as one piece.
Slots are 100 px apart: slot k is at x = 250 + 100 * k. Bar height = 38 px per unit, standing on y = 470.
A lifted bar (y = -240) floats above the others while they shift.
insertion-sort.title: How insertionSort() works
insertion-sort.description: Grows a sorted part on the left, inserting one element at a time.

slides.caption: insertionSort grows a sorted part on the left (green line). It takes the next element and slides it left into place.
Next element: 2.
5 is bigger than 2, so 5 shifts one place right and 2 drops into the gap. Sorted part: [2, 5].
Next element: 4.
5 > 4 shifts right. 2 < 4, so the shifting stops and 4 goes after 2. Sorted part: [2, 4, 5].
Next element: 6. It is bigger than 5, so nothing moves. Sorted part: [2, 4, 5, 6].
Next element: 1, the smallest so far.
6, 5, 4 and 2 are all bigger than 1, so each one shifts one place right.
1 drops into the first slot. Sorted part: [1, 2, 4, 5, 6].
Last element: 3.
6, 5 and 4 shift right. 2 is smaller than 3, so the shifting stops there.
3 goes into the gap and the whole array is sorted: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6].

factorial.//: The call stack: each call is a group (box + text). New calls appear on top.
factorial.title: How factorial() works
factorial.description: A recursive call stack that grows down to the base case and then unwinds.

slides.caption: factorial(n) multiplies n by factorial(n - 1). To compute factorial(4), it first needs factorial(3).
So factorial(4) waits, and a call to factorial(3) goes on top of it.
factorial(3) needs factorial(2): one more call on the stack.
factorial(2) needs factorial(1).
factorial(1) is the base case: it returns 1 without calling itself again. Now the stack unwinds.
slides.//: pause here so the viewer can take in the full stack

slides.caption: factorial(1) is done and leaves the stack. factorial(2) can finish: 2 × 1 = 2.
factorial(3) = 3 × 2 = 6.
factorial(4) = 4 × 6 = 24. The stack is empty again and 24 is the result.

stack-new.//: Slots stand on top of each other: slot k is at y = 470 - 75 * k.
stack-new.title: new IntStack(capacity)
stack-new.description: Creates an empty stack with a fixed number of slots.

slides.caption: new IntStack(4) creates an empty stack that can hold up to 4 values.
It reserves 4 slots, numbered from the bottom (0) to the top (3).
There are no values yet: size = 0. push() fills the slots from the bottom up.

stack-push.title: How push() works
stack-push.description: Puts a value on top of the stack.

slides.caption: push(value) puts a new value on top of the stack. Right now it holds 3 and 8, so size = 2.
push(5): the value goes into slot number size = 2, the first free slot.
It lands on top of 8.
size becomes 3 and 5 is the new top. The last value pushed is always the first one popped.
One slot is still free. When all 4 are full, push throws IllegalStateException.

stack-pop.title: How pop() works
stack-pop.description: Removes the value on top and returns it.

slides.caption: pop() removes the value on top and returns it. The stack holds 3, 8 and 5, so size = 3.
The top value is in slot size - 1 = 2: it is 5.
5 is taken off the stack and returned to the caller.
size becomes 2, so 8 is the new top. Calling pop() again would return 8.
On an empty stack there is nothing to return, so pop() throws IllegalStateException.
